title: ASIRT clears Edmonton police officers who killed bystander while firing on robbery suspect
article: The sister of a man killed by a stray bullet fired by an Edmonton police officer is upset after the release of a report by Alberta's police watchdog clearing the officers of criminal wrongdoing.

The Alberta Serious Incident Response Team (ASIRT) released its long-awaited decision on Wednesday in the Feb. 23, 2022, shooting outside a central Edmonton apartment building that killed Mitchell Tyler Potts - an armed robbery suspect carrying an imitation shotgun - and James Hanna - an apartment caretaker shot through the window of his basement suite.

ASIRT concluded while there may be issues that can be addressed through training, there are no grounds to believe any of the officers who fired in the direction of Hanna's building that night committed a criminal offence.
Norm Assiff, who is representing Hanna's estate, said Hanna's sister, Susan Bandola, is "angrier and left with more questions than answers" in the wake of the ASIRT report.
"This was expected to bring some closure to the family; the exact opposite is what was achieved by a 13-page report that took nearly three years."

Potts was suspected of robbing a liquor store at 113 Street and 104 Avenue in the lead-up to the shooting. Police were told a male suspect was carrying what appeared to be a gun and threatened to shoot anyone who followed him. Police spotted the suspect in a bus shelter at 104 Street and 107 Avenue half an hour later.

Police pursued and repeatedly ordered him to drop the gun. The suspect ran across the LRT tracks at 105 Street, turned, and pointed the suspected gun at the pursuing officers. The three officers opened fire, and the suspect fell to the ground.

A second group of officers approached Potts and began first aid, but he died of his injuries. Another officer then went to check the nearby apartment building - about 40 feet behind Potts when police opened fire - and noticed several stray bullet holes, including through a ground-floor window.

When the officers looked through the window, they saw a man slumped motionless in a chair, ASIRT said. They entered the apartment, kicked in the door, and found Hanna mortally injured from a bullet wound in the centre of his chest. He died in hospital.
One of the officers noticed another bullet hole coming from inside the apartment through the wall into the hallway. He knocked on the door of another suite and determined no one inside was injured.

An autopsy determined Hanna died of a single round of an EPS carbine to the chest. Potts also died of gunshot wounds and had alcohol, fentanyl, and methamphetamine in his blood at the time of death. The suspected firearm he pointed at officers turned out to be a BB gun.

The three officers who opened fire on Potts are not identified in ASIRT's report. Two were armed with carbines while one carried a pistol. ASIRT could not determine which of the carbine-carrying officers fired the round that killed Hanna.

ASIRT ultimately found 12 carbine casings and six pistol casings at the scene but added the search was hampered by recent snow. Three rounds were found in a barrier between the apartment and the LRT tracks while another six were determined to have struck the building exterior outside Hanna's suite. ASIRT executive director Michael Ewenson said it was not possible to determine where the bullet that killed Hanna entered the building, given the likelihood the round changed trajectories.
He said it's possible the bullet that killed Hanna wasn't an "errant round" at all, noting the majority of the 12 rounds that struck Potts left his body.

"Two grazing wounds, eight through and through, and one wound that exited, re-entered and exited again," Ewenson summarized. "It is possible that a round that went through (Potts), entered (Hanna's) apartment and then struck him."

Ewenson concluded the officers did not break any laws by opening fire that night. He said that while Potts was carrying an imitation firearm, "this item looks like a real gun," and the officers at the scene that night were reasonable in making that conclusion.
Hanna's death was "completely unintended" and "extremely tragic," he said.

ASIRT considered whether criminal negligence charges would be warranted, but Ewenson said the standard established by the Supreme Court is that a person's actions must be "a marked and substantial departure from what a reasonable prudent person would do under the circumstances."

"A police officer's use of force, in law, is not to be assessed on a standard of perfection nor using the benefit of hindsight, and the opportunity to consider alternatives with the luxury of time," Ewenson wrote, "recognizing the exigencies of the circumstances and the decisions and reactions that must occur in split seconds."
Ewenson concluded the officers' actions were defensible under Section 25 of the Criminal Code, which covers the use of force by police officers, as well as the self-defence provisions in Section 34.
He said the officers were lawfully placed and acting to protect the public from an apparently armed man who had committed two robberies.

Whether Hanna's death may have been prevented through changes in training, resources or equipment - including the type of ammunition given to patrol officers - are "not within ASIRT's mandate" and are "commonly examined" through other processes, including fatality inquiries, Ewenson said.

In a statement, Edmonton Police Service spokesperson Carolin Maran called Hanna's death "the tragic loss of an innocent bystander" and acknowledged "the ongoing grief caused by his passing. We continue to send our condolences to his loved ones."

"The EPS also appreciates ASIRT's thorough review of this incident and its support of our officers in the findings that they were lawfully placed and assessed the public safety risks appropriately given the circumstances," she said.

"These incidents have a profound impact on our members, the community, and attending first responders. Knowing the use or presence of an imitation firearm was a root of this tragedy, reinforces the need to remind Edmontonians that officers cannot tell if a firearm is real or fake, but the consequences of their improper and threatening use can be tragic, as they were here."
Maran said EPS' professional standards branch will now consider whether the officers will be investigated for misconduct under the Police Act. She declined to comment further, citing the civil case.
